newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq and U.N., U.S. exchange complaints on food plan.
newsitem.headline: Iraq and U.N., U.S. exchange complaints on food plan.

text.p: Iraq on Tuesday complained that food supplies under an "oil-for-food" plan were taking too long to arrive while U.N. sources said Baghdad was hindering operations on the ground.

And in Washington State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns placed the entire blame on Iraq saying that it was "delaying access to transportation and communications by the U.N. monitors and are denying the U.N. monitors the full freedom of movement the U.N. was promised."

U.N. officials earlier made the same complaints as Burns but said this did not account for the fact that no supplies had arrived in Iraq, which was due mainly to the carefully spelled out procedures for approving contracts.

At issue is an "oil-for-food" agreement that took effect on Dec. 10 and permits Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other necessities to offset the effects of sanctions imposed after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

After seeing Secretary-General Kofi Annan late on Monday Iraq's U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon appealed to non-aligned members of the Security Council on Tuesday to support his demand for speedier delivery of food supplies.
In response, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan had promised to give Iraq more details on the deliveries and asked Hamdoon to relay U.N. operational problems to Baghdad.
The United Nations is currently sending 155 monitors to Iraq to ensure equitable distribution of the supplies.

Once they and the goods arrive, some diplomats expect further difficulties between Iraq and the monitors. In addition U.N. staff have been late in organizing the monitoring mission after some squabbling between departments.

Hamdoon said "no kilo of rice or sugar or whatever has really arrived in Iraq," He said the Security Council's sanctions committee was slow in approving them and that procedures were "very cumbersome and time-consuming."
Taking up Iraq's complaint, Russia asked U.N. officials to brief the Security Council this week on precisely what supplies were en rute and when they would reach Iraq.

Eckhard said oil sales had reached $386 million but only $113 million had been dispersed. Four contracts for foodstuffs were approved: $21 million for French wheat, $50 million for Australian wheat, $21 million for Thai rice and $5.5 million for tea from Jordan.

The sanctions commitee considered 10 applications, blocked one and put five others on hold, he said. But he said the United Nations had received 131 applications from vendors selling food, medicine and other goods and U.N. staff passed the applications to the sanctions committee depending on the funds available from oil revenues.

Hamdoon told reporters on Monday he asked Annan to let Baghdad know why contracts were rejected so Iraq could make sure technical matters were resolved. He said Iraq also wanted to decide which contracts should be substituted in place of those rejected.
